title: Two Sum
keyIdea: For each number, the partner it needs is fixed: rem = target − nums[i]. Keep a map of number → index for everything already passed; if rem is in it, that's the pair. Look up first, then save, so a number never pairs with itself.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try every pair (i, j) with i < j and return the first one that adds up to target.
approaches.why: n·(n−1)/2 pairs. With n up to 10⁴ that's about 5·10⁷ checks: passes, but it's the answer the interviewer wants you to improve.

approaches.name: Sort + two pointers
approaches.idea: Sort (value, index) pairs, then squeeze from both ends: sum too small → move left up, too big → move right down.
approaches.why: Sorting dominates. The pairs vector is needed because sorting would lose the original indices the answer asks for.
approaches.warn: Only worth it when the array is already sorted (that's LC 167, where it's O(1) space). Here the hash map is simpler and faster.

approaches.name: Hash map, one pass
approaches.idea: Walk once. rem = target − nums[i]. If seen has rem, return {seen[rem], i}. Otherwise save seen[nums[i]] = i.
approaches.why: Each number does one count() and one insert, both O(1) on average. The map can hold up to n numbers.

quiz.q: Why does the map store number → index and not index → number?
options: You look up by the number you need (rem) and want back where it was

quiz.q: Why check seen.count(rem) before seen[nums[i]] = i?
options: So a number can't pair with itself (e.g. 3 with target 6 in [3,2,4])
i=0: 3 not found, save 3→0. i=1: rem 3 found → {0,1}

quiz.q: When is sort + two pointers the better choice?
options: When the array is already sorted (LC 167): O(n) time, O(1) space
